newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec unveils plan to regulate gasoline prices.
newsitem.headline: Quebec unveils plan to regulate gasoline prices.

text.p: Quebec's government said Thursday it would present legislation giving it sweeping powers to regulate gasoline prices in the province.
Under the government plans, outlined by Quebec Energy Minister Guy Chevrette, gasoline retailers would be forced to charge prices at the pump using a minimum profit margin.
The move came after price wars this past summer, triggered by Ultramar Corp., Quebec's largest seller of gasoline, caused independent retailers to complain their livelihoods were threatened.
The ruling Parti Quebecois government said in August, after prices fell to their lowest levels, that it was considering regulatory action on gasoline prices.
Under the proposed legislation, a new agency, the Quebec Energy Board, would be created to monitor and enforce prices.
"This series of measures have been adopted to permit sane competition in this sector, that has been at several times the scene of price wars," Chevrette told reporters.

He said the moves would mean that major oil companies -- which in Quebec include Imperial Oil Ltd., Shell Canada Ltd., Petro-Canada and Ultramar Canada Ltd. -- would be prohibited from posting prices at the pumps below those charged to independent retailers for resale.

"As a government, we have a duty to maintain the equilibrium between the interest of the consumers, who want to obtain prices as low as possible, and the survival of small independent retailers that create 10,000 jobs in Quebec," Chevrette said.

Gasoline prices, which have recently been around 50 cents to 60 cents Canadian per litre ($1.38-$1.66 per gallon) in most Canadian regions, dropped to as low as C19 cents per litre (53 cents per gallon) in the Montreal area in July.
